Dropsy
DROP-see
noun
A worn form of the Middle English ydropesie, from the Greek hudrops, “watery,” from hudor, “water”; the disease in which water gathers in the body, swelling the limbs and belly with a thirst no drinking can quench.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The dropsy is the water-sickness — a body swollen and waterlogged, heavy, and tormented by a thirst that drinking only worsens. Luke the physician alone records the case, and he sets it in a room full of watching enemies: “And it came to pass, as he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the sabbath day, that they watched him. And, behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy” (Luk 14:1–2). The man stood there like a trap set and baited. Christ did not evade it; He sprang it first: “And Jesus answering spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?” (Luk 14:3). They held their peace, for the question had no answer that would not condemn them. “And he took him, and healed him, and let him go” (Luk 14:4). Then He turned their own practice upon their consciences: “Which of you shall have an ass or an ox fallen into a pit, and will not straightway pull him out on the sabbath day?” (Luk 14:5). They would haul a beast out of a hole on the LORD’s day and grudge a man his health. The sabbath was made for man, and the Lord of the sabbath keeps it best who heals on it. The dropsical man asked nothing, said nothing, and went home whole.

Webster 1828 Definition

A morbid collection of water in the body or its parts; the swelling, water-sickness with its unquenchable thirst.

expand to see more

DROPSY, an unnatural collection of water in any part of the body, attended with swelling and with a thirst not relieved by drinking.

From Middle English ydropesie, Greek hudrops, “watery,” from hudor, water.

It is the disease of a man full of water and dying of thirst — a parable in flesh.

Luke, the beloved physician, alone names it (Luk 14:2).

Christ healed it on the sabbath before lawyers and Pharisees who had set the case as a snare.

Key Scripture

Luk 14:2 — "And, behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy."

Luk 14:3 — "And Jesus answering spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?"

Luk 14:4 — "And they held their peace. And he took him, and healed him, and let him go;"

Luk 14:1 — "And it came to pass, as he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the sabbath day, that they watched him."

Modern Corruption

A one-verse disease that exposes two errors about the LORD’s day — the legalism that forbids mercy on it, and the laxity that forbids nothing at all.

expand to see more

The Pharisees’ error was to make the fourth commandment a fence against mercy. They had multiplied rules until a swollen man could not be healed and a hungry disciple could not rub an ear of corn, and they sat watching the Son of God to see whether He would do good, that they might accuse Him for it. That spirit is not extinct. Wherever the LORD’s day is kept as a performance of scruples rather than a delight in God, and wherever a congregation is more scandalised by a broken custom than by a neighbour left in his misery, the lawyers of Luke 14 are still at table. Christ’s question is the permanent rebuke: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day? They held their peace, because the law they claimed to guard was on His side and not on theirs.

But the opposite error is the one our own age commits, and it is worse. Having heard that Christ healed on the sabbath, the modern professor concludes that the day means nothing — that the Christian sabbath is a Jewish relic, and the LORD’s day a slot in the schedule to be filled with commerce, sport, and errands, church attended when convenient. That is not liberty; it is the loss of a creation ordinance and a covenant gift. The 1689 Confession holds the Christian sabbath as a positive, moral, perpetual commandment, changed to the first day of the week in memory of Christ’s resurrection, kept by a holy resting from worldly employments and recreations, and taken up with worship and with the duties of necessity and mercy. The dropsical man is precisely the duty of mercy. Christ did not abolish the day; He cleared it of Pharisees and filled it with healing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means “watery” — the body swollen with water and burning with thirst.

expand to see more

Dropsy — Middle English ydropesie, from Greek hudrops, “watery.”

Root hudor, “water” — the same root behind our hydrant and hydraulic.

The sufferer is full of water and thirsty still — drinking increases the disease.

A KJV hapax, recorded only by Luke the physician (Luk 14:2).

Its healing is the fourth of Luke’s sabbath-day miracles and the sharpest.

Usage

"The dropsy: full of water, and thirsty still — the very picture of the sinner in his pleasures."

"Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day? — and they held their peace."

"He took him, and healed him, and let him go: no debate, no apology, no delay."
